To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the human mirror neuron (MNS) system is a crucial component of an observer’s response to an observed action but that it is not the only component, as other brain areas are also recruited when a complementary response is required.

the human mirror neuron network appears to be involved in the process that leads to complementary responses in social situations, but that other neural networks are also recruited to achieve this end.
complementary action is the result of a switch between two neural mechanisms that are both involved in action understanding: the human mirror neuron and the action-effect prediction systems.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the neural mechanisms underlying the switch from the imitative to the complementary mode of responding to observed actions.
how the human brain processes observed actions in order to produce appropriate responses in social contexts.
the mechanisms that underlie the ability to respond to observed actions in a context-appropriate manner.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
complementary actions are not necessarily executed by the human mirror neuron systems, but that this system plays an important role in the process.
complementary behavior emerges from the interplay of several neural systems, including those involved in action observation and those involved in the execution of context-appropriate actions.
, although the human mirror neuron network is a crucial component in the process of switching from imitating to complementing, other neural structures might also contribute to this switch.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
complementary responses are generated through the interplay between the human mirror neuron and other brain systems.
complementary behavior is a product of the human mirror system and its interaction with the other systems in the brain.
complementary responses to observed actions are not the default outcome of action perception, but rather the product of an active process of decision making.
The main takeaway from our work is that

complementary actions are not just the result of a simple switch in the motor system, but rather the result of an interaction between the mirror neuron system and other neural systems that are recruited in a context-specific fashion.
the human mirror neuron network is not the only brain region that is recruited during action observation.
the human mirror neuron network is not a unitary entity, and that it is not only the case that the human mirror system does not always mirror, but that it does not mirror the same thing all the time.
